#4848. The 6 Best Rowing Machines for Your Gym, Tested by Fitness Experts

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

WHEN IT COMES to your fitness routine, it can be nice to switch things up. If you don't own one already, an indoor rowing machine is a piece of equipment you can count on for a high-payoff, low-impact (AKA joint-friendly) workout at home. We've got several in the Men's Health gym, and many of our editors have one or even two at home and use them regularly for this very reason. This might be just the total-body workout you've been looking for.

Indoor rowing is an excellent way to improve cardiovascular fitness and muscular endurance. Since it is a low-impact sport, rowing reduces the risk of damage to weight-bearing joints, such as hips, ankles, and knees, which tend to be prone to injury and soreness when doing high-impact sports. But rowing's not just a great joint-friendly form of cardio. A solid rowing workout can also help build strength in more muscle groups than you'd expect.

"The rower is basically the horizontal version of the deadlift and uses similar muscles," says veteran trainer Ian Creighton. "On the drive, the main focus is on the posterior chain—the hamstrings, glutes, calves, and spinal erectors are all being used. In the pull, the quads, forearms, biceps, and lats are used as well."

Indoor rowing machines are a bit more complicated than ordinary home gym equipment, like weight benches or dumbbell sets. Decades ago, they used to be little more than a gliding seat and rope handle attached to a water-filled flywheel. But today’s best rowing machines are a lot more high-tech and sophisticated. That’s to say, shopping for a new rower can be a challenge. We’re here to help with the most important specs, features, and essentials to consider before forking over your hard-earned money. If cost is a major concern, check out our story on the best rowing machines under $500.

Over the past three years, we've tested every major rower on the market, yet the Concept2 RowErg still reigns supreme. Its high-quality construction, easy assembly, and incredibly smooth ride make the RowErg the best in its class. And at this price point, we think it offers many of the same features as the best rowing machines that cost twice as much.

In fact, this piece of home gym equipment is an industry standard used by CrossFit and many high-profile competitions. Our Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, CSCS, says this is his go-to rowing machine because it can blast your abs, glutes, and back while redlining your heart rate. "It's built for either long cardio workouts or vicious high-intensity sessions," he says.

The RowErg has a durable construction that can support people up to 500 pounds. Our editors have used the RowErg in their home gyms for years and found it still works like new. We also appreciate the variable-resistance flywheel, which provides a consistent challenge. Our fitness editors say this feature is especially useful for high-volume use and experienced rowers.

It's easy to assemble, too. In our experience setting up this rower, it takes about 15 minutes, ideally with two people, and minimal tools or hardware (just eight screws). I set mine up myself with no issue, and it took no longer than 10 minutes. Not trying to brag or anything, but it was easy. (I posted a video about the assembly here). Plus, it separates into two pieces for easy storage, making it a great option for people with smaller home gym setups.

Yes, it lacks smart connectivity and the big, beautiful LED screens found in newer models like the Hydrow, but if you're looking for a tough-as-nails machine that can keep up with your toughest workouts, the RowErg delivers the definitive home rowing experience. That's why it's our pick for the best rowing machine of 2026.

Read More: Our Hands-On Review of the Concept2 RowErg

"If I can’t use a Concept2, this is my go-to," says Samuel. The Hydrow Wave is a more streamlined and slimmed-down version of Hydrow's original Rower Connected Rowing Machine—and a 2025 Men's Health Fitness Awards winner. It's a smart machine with an HD screen that features immersive guided workouts to recreate a real-world rowing experience. And after using the Wave Rower for over a year now, we can attest that it delivers on that promise.

The electromagnetic resistance is incredibly smooth and quiet, and Hydrow's armada of on-demand classes are surprisingly lifelike. "It feels as if you're out on the water, complete with videos shot on lakes and rivers," says Samuel. "The end result: a tranquil row seat." While other cardio machines we've tested got repetitive after a few weeks of use, Hydrow's video programs always kept things interesting.

This rower fits easily in my basement training area, and can stand up for storage. Not only does it fold, but it looks good folded up. Despite the compact size, we've found the Wave is also SUPER-durable: I can go hard on this rower for sprints, or take on longer intervals without it struggling to keep up.

We do wish this rower had a free mode to allow users to build their own workouts. Despite that, this is the best magnetic resistance rowing experience on the market. If you're someone who cares about the details and wants to learn from experts, this is the best pick for you.

Hydrow's pricing is usually the same on Amazon as anywhere else, but if you want to see a full list of add-ons, you might want to purchase one on their website.

Read More: Our Review of the Hydrow Wave Rower

Whether you're competing live against your peers, trying to out-row world-class athletes, or even being chased by a deadly Kraken, the Strong Series Rower is a fix for boring rowing workouts. Aside from the basics (like tracking performance stats), a massive and crisp definition 22-inch touchscreen allows for streaming content from Netflix, Hulu, Disney+, Prime Video, Spotify, and YouTube, as well as a library of interactive, performance-based video games.

The tech was actually developed by game designers using game psychology, with the singular goal of encouraging rowing performance. The animated games are immersive and easy to learn, and incentivize players to increase output in creative ways.

Aside from the gamified perks, one major feature of this machine is its 20-inch elevated seat, which makes it easy for beginners, older individuals, and those with limited mobility to get on and off the machine. It isn't as low to the ground as more traditional rowing machines, and is therefore more accessible for some people.

The foot pedals are also more wide-set and larger than found on most rowers, which makes it feel more accessible for a range of users. For bigger individuals who typically feel crammed or awkward on a standard machine, this is for you. But that doesn't mean it takes up more room. In fact, this rower can be flipped upright easily and stored without a wall mount.

Read More: Exercises to Improve Your Rowing

Sometimes simpler is just better. The made-in-the-USA design takes things back to basics with a vaguely vintage aesthetic of stained ash wood. There is no denying that in certain homes the aesthetic of a wooden water rower is just superior. This also makes it one of the most heavy-duty machines in this guide, supporting users up to 700 pounds.

We found that the traditional water-based flywheel not only looks great, but does an incredible job of recreating the feel of rowing through real water. Users can fully customize the resistance by filling the water tank with more or less water, which can make a mess, but isn't difficult to do. Keep in mind you'll also need to treat the water on a consistent basis so it doesn't get moldy.

At around $1,400, this model lacks the fancier gadgetry of the pricier models in our guide. So if you don't rely heavily on video classes or virtual instructors for your motivation then you can save a good amount by going with this simpler machine. Still, the integrated performance monitor tracks all the essentials.

The absence of a screen also means that this piece of equipment can be folded upright and stored easier than most, meaning it's perfect for putting away in closets or corners. For anyone looking for a durable, handsome rower without unnecessary bells and whistles at a good price, this is your pick.

The top-rated Ergatta Rower (a Men's Health Fitness Awards winner) is all performance, complete with game-based workouts that challenge you daily. It's the most "gamified" water-based rowing machine we've tested with a long list of virtual workout programs to choose from. We took it for a spin with head-to-head races, high-intensity endurance workouts, and goal-based gamified training plans to get the full experience.

We found this is one of the smoothest water rowers we've used, and the games are enough to keep things fun and interesting even when doing a basic workout. The game-based workouts felt like a much-needed changeup from typical hard workouts on a Concept2, and are actually good for dialing in form.

In terms of the frame, the lone downside is that the feet are positioned a little more closely than we prefer. But on the plus side, rolling this model and folding it is easy. Not only that, but it looks cool even when folded up against the wall.

The warm cherry wood feels extremely durable and gives the rower a sleek retro-modern aesthetic that elevated the look of our home gym space. It's among the priciest rowing machines in this guide, but if you're in the market for a top-of-the-line rower that doubles as a home accessory, it's hard to beat.

Men’s Health fitness writer and strength coach David Otey, CSCS, took the Peloton Cross Training Row+ for a spin and confirmed that it’s set to give every rower in our guide—even the most goated rowing machines—a run for their money.

Otey and MH fitness editors found both the seat and foot pedals extremely comfortable, and the foot strap secure yet easy to adjust with a single hand. Otey describes the strap’s pull as "silky smooth" without the annoying catching found in lesser rowers. We found that the electrically-controlled resistance also makes for whisper-quiet operation.

But the real star isn't its frame. "Peloton's best asset isn't its hardware; it's a great software company," Otey says. The tech on this machine delivers, with a Form Assist function that can help nearly any level rower achieve better form as they row.

It’s not perfect, however. Otey notes that its most obvious shortcoming is the lack of an adjustable manual mode. This is a stark difference from many manual rowers, which shows Peloton is more confident in their programming and instructors than your ability to create your own workouts.

The rower can be easily stored vertically against a wall, but requires an anchor to go into the wall for safety. This is perfect for any rowers looking for great classes and a well-built machine, especially if they are already Peloton fans.

When considering an indoor rowing machine, you'll encounter a variety of resistance systems.

If you’re dropping $1,000 or more on a complicated piece of gym equipment, you want to know that it can go the distance. That’s why it pays (literally) to buy from a company that you trust and that offers a solid, reputable product with a decent warranty. Don’t settle for a bargain-priced Amazon model from a brand you’ve never heard of just because it seems like a steal. In the world of fitness equipment, you almost always get what you pay for. If you’re planning to row on a regular basis and to keep your rowing machine for the foreseeable future, consider investing good money into a model that will last.

By their nature, rowing machines are big, bulky, and often heavy. If you have the real estate in your home, non-folding models are typically sturdier and more convenient when it comes time to work out. They’re always set up and ready to go—er, row. If you’re a city dweller or are just short on space, however, a folding rowing machine might be the best way to go. Some rowers fold neatly in half or offer vertical storage to minimize wasted floor space. Look for models with transport wheels so you can easily move yours around by yourself.

With the best rowing machines priced north of $1,000, buying one is a serious investment. So, it’s important to purchase from a manufacturer that offers a clear, comprehensive warranty. They vary widely across the industry, with the most budget-forward brands offering just 90 days on some parts, and others boasting generous 10-year warranties on everything. Again, the more you spend upfront, the better the warranty is likely to be. And, if there’s anything that isn’t clear to you about the stated warranty, be sure to ask. It’s your money, after all.

The most basic rowing machine design has changed little in decades, and you can still find a “classic”-style model for a reasonable price. But, if you’re looking for a more connected experience, look at smart rowers like the Hydrow Wave or the Peloton Row. These offer touchscreens with built-in apps that connect you to professional trainers who can motivate and work with you to better achieve your personal goals. The rowing machines with these features are, of course, more expensive upfront. But, know that many also require ongoing monthly subscriptions to take full advantage of those “smart” connected features.

As the Fitness and Reviews Editor of Men's Health, it's my job to test the latest and greatest in fitness equipment, including rowing machines. My fellow Men's Health fitness editors and experts included but weren't limited to Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, CSCS, Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM, David Otey, CSCS, and Ian Creighton.

Our methodology for assessing the best rowing machines for home use involved thorough testing across performance, build quality, comfort, features, resistance mechanism, and user experience. We conducted extensive performance and stress tests with over two dozen rowing machines through rowing workouts of varying lengths and intensities, and paid close attention to comfort and user-friendly features along the way. We used these rowers through hundreds of miles of testing for warm-ups, cardio burns, HIIT workouts, endurance training, and finishers. Features such as resistance levels, workout programs, and connectivity were scrutinized in detail.

After we had examined each individually, we had our final picks shipped to The Garage Gym in Westfield, New Jersey, to stack them all against each other, literally. Here's our guide to the best rowing machines for your home right now.

Our fitness experts love indoor machines for a ton of reasons. But the biggest one is how easy and accessible they are for enthusiasts of any fitness level. Seriously, there’s not much more to using one than simply sitting down and pulling—rinse and repeat. But like any workout machine, there is a right way and a wrong way. The best way to not only maximize your performance and rowing gains but also to avoid injury is to practice the proper rowing technique.

Start by sitting squarely on the seat with your tailbone pointing directly into the middle. Follow your rowing stroke through each of these four phases, paying careful attention to your posture and form:

To start, your shins should be perpendicular to the floor (i.e., vertical). Extend your arms fully—with a focus on your triceps—and grab the rower’s handle. Be mindful of your core, and slightly lean your torso forward.

While keeping your arms straight, power through the Drive phase with your leg muscles, pushing your body (and the seat) smoothly away from the footplates. Finish by pulling the handle into your abdomen and leaning back.

Despite the name, you’re not quite "finished." In this phase, your elbows should be bent and the handle tucked into the lower part of your chest. Use your core to stabilize your torso, keeping a slight angle toward the rowing machine.

Be mindful of your form while returning to the starting position in this phase. Straighten your arms by using your triceps. Slightly lean your torso forward. Bend your legs and smoothly slide your butt and the seat down the rail of the rowing machine.

Once back in the starting position, repeat the next stroke by beginning with the Drive phase again.

Rowing is a near-perfect exercise, and a good indoor rowing machine promises a low-impact, full-body workout with the convenience of a single device. “Since rowing promotes improvements to both your muscular strength and cardiovascular strength, you get two for one,” says Tuttle. She outlines four specific reasons why you should buy a rowing machine:

“A proper warmup is key to having a successful workout; it should prepare your heart, muscles, joints, and mind for the harder efforts to come,” says Tuttle. Because it’s so low-impact, it’s a great slow warm-up, even if rowing isn’t your ultimate program goal on a given day.

Because rowing is significantly lower impact than most high-intensity exercises like running, it’s far easier to recover between workouts. Ideally, a rowing machine will help add variety to your workout days.

Because indoor rowing involves fewer external stimuli than outdoor activities, it can be extremely meditative. Tuttle agrees: “Once warm and a comfortable rhythm has been established, you can close your eyes, connect your breath to your body, and simply enjoy the gift of movement,” she says.

Hardcore workout sessions often involve an explosive finish. Hopping on your rowing machine near the end of your routine is a great way to cap things off. “It's hard to pass up a good 5- to 10-minute long EMOM (Every Minute On the Minute) row 100 to 200 meters, depending upon your fitness and skill level,” says Tuttle. “Each effort should be about 90 percent max intensity and your goal is to finish with 20 seconds or more to recover before the top of the next minute.”

If a low-impact cardio machine is what you're looking for, it's true that indoor bikes and rowers can both be suitable options. The best choice for you? Well, it all comes down to your goals.

The rowing machine provides a full-body workout that engages multiple muscle groups. However, it requires a technique and coordination to avoid injury and that can be less intuitive for some users compared to using an exercise bike. Rowers also take up more space and can be noisy.

On the other hand, stationary bikes can provide a great cardio workout, are more adjustable (seat height, handlebars, etc.) and are easy to use. But biking primarily focuses on lower-body muscles, and may not challenge the upper body or coordination as effectively as a rowing machine.

In general, says Samuel, the rower will be the more advanced cardio option. According to him, the rower delivers a more “well-rounded” workout. It also directly challenges your mid-back muscles, lower back muscles, and glutes.

“These are all key postural muscles,” Samuel told us, “so you’re getting extra benefits out of the rower.”

The downside: Rowing also requires more technique, so there’s a higher learning curve to dominating on the rower.

The best way to avoid getting injured on the rower is to master proper technique, according to Samuel. You'll want to tighten your abs before each pull, and aim to let your legs drive the motion. He recommends working hard not to lean back too aggressively as you finish each row stroke; think of your torso shifting between a 10 o'clock angle and 2 o'clock as you row. Anything more than that isn't beneficial.

Additionally, start every row workout with a brief warmup. This doesn't need to take long, but before you start pulling to the max during any workout, spend at least a minute doing slower, controlled pulls through the full range of your rowing motion, driving blood flow and gradually elevating your heart rate. That'll get you primed to row your best.

Finally, make sure there's plenty of room on every side of the rower. Having three feet of space on either side of the rower will allow you to comfortably pull your arms backward even if your elbows flare. You'll want five to seven feet behind the rower, giving you room to shift your torso backward on every stride. And keep a few feet in front of the rower, too. And remember, if you're rowing hard, your heart rate will climb up there. So, don’t forget a decent cool-down.

Targeted fat loss has been proven to be virtually impossible. But rowing machines are great for almost every aspect of fitness, including building strength, lowering overall body fat, increasing stamina, and even weight loss. The reason is simple: By burning a ton of calories (putting yourself in a calorie deficit), you can more easily score a negative daily energy balance. Bottom line: You’re consuming fewer calories than you’re burning. Maintaining a calorie deficit over a long period is the guiding principle behind successfully losing weight and keeping it off.

Charles Thorp is the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, where he shares the best product recommendations in gym equipment, recovery tools, supplements, and more. Following an early life in athletics, Charles became a NASM-certified trainer and began writing programs alongside the most respected coaches in the world.   Since entering the world of fitness content, Charles has had the opportunity to learn from and train alongside high performance individuals from the NFL, UFC, NBA, Formula 1, CrossFit, US Olympics, and Navy SEALs. When he’s not writing about training programs or gear, he can be seen at the gym or in the wild, putting them to the test.

David Otey, CSCS is a fitness writer, NYC-based strength coach, and Men's Health Advisory Board member who specializes in strength and hypertrophy protocols as well as athletic performance. For more on Otey check out www.oteyfitness.com.

Ian Creighton is the Chief Marketing Officer at Honeycomb Wellness, formerly the general manager at Brick New York, the largest functional fitness facility in Manhattan, and a personal trainer to high level business executives, Hollywood movie producers, and actors. A recovering CrossFit addict, he now spends his time focused on optimizing longevity and takes a "functional bodybuilding" approach to training.

#4846. I Went to Gee’s Bend to See Its Famous Quilts. Nothing Prepared Me for the Beauty

I chew my tongue, concentrating on keeping my needle from wandering off its line. Over my shoulder, Doris Pettway Mosely watches my hands with the patience of someone who has been quilting since she was 11. She gently corrects my angle and sewing style, while Mary Margaret Pettway does the same for the rest of our small class. We laugh through most of it. Then Doris looks over my work and tells me my stitches are nice and short, and I sit up a little straighter.

I’m spending my morning at the fifth annual Airing of the Quilts Festival in Gee’s Bend, Alabama, where two of the community’s most celebrated quilters are teaching a roomful of beginners how to stitch 12-by-12-inch quilt squares. Mary Margaret, a fourth-generation quilter, has shown her work in major museums across the country. Doris, the daughter of celebrated quilter Leola Pettway, still sews her mother’s signature Z pattern alongside her own vivid, scrap-pieced designs. “I learned at four years old,” Mary Margaret tells me, explaining that she picked up the craft from her mother, Lucy T. Pettway. In their house, quilting was a chore like mopping or sweeping the yard, and the boys learned too.

Colorful booths at the Airing of the Quilts Festival in Gee’s Bend, Alabama

After class, I wander the festival grounds, where quilts hang from clotheslines strung between wooden posts. A quilt of nested squares in navy and sky blue hangs next to one in butter yellow, punched with blocks of chartreuse and red. Another glows neon coral. Farther down the line, rings of pale pink, olive green, and rose-print fabric radiate out from a single center square, a take on the classic Housetop pattern. Inside the River Gallery, a quilt called Remembering Dinah is pieced from faded denim and mustard corduroy, its back pockets and frayed knees left intact. It’s a reminder of where this tradition began.

Children learning to quilt in Gee’s Bend, Alabama, in 2010

Today, Gee’s Bend quilts hang in more than 40 museums, but they began as something far more practical. This small town takes its name from Joseph Gee, who established a cotton plantation in this bend of the Alabama River in 1816. Enslaved people and generations of their descendants stitched quilts to keep their families warm during winter and to brighten their homes, piecing them together from worn-out work clothes, denim, and whatever fabric scraps they had. Each year as summer gave way to fall, women hung their quilts outside to air before the cold set in, a tradition that inspired the Airing of the Quilts Festival, launched in 2022 by nonprofit organizations Freedom Quilting Bee Legacy and Sew Gee’s Bend Heritage Builders.

A quilt on display in Gee’s Bend, Alabama

Among the community’s earliest known named quilters was Dinah Miller, who was taken from West Africa as a girl in 1860, likely aboard the Clotilda, the last known slave ship to reach the US. She settled in Gee’s Bend in the 1890s and passed her craft down. During the civil rights movement, the quilts became a financial lifeline. Black residents who tried to register to vote risked losing their jobs and the land they lived on to white landowners. In 1962, officials shut down the ferry connecting the community to the county seat, making it difficult to register to vote, and cutting them off from grocery stores, banks, schools, and medical care. The ferry didn’t run again until 2006.

Four years after the closure, the community established the Freedom Quilting Bee, a cooperative that gave local women an income their white employers couldn’t take away. When Father Francis X. Walter, an Episcopal priest and Mobile native, saw the bold quilts on a trip to Wilcox County, he helped organize auctions in New York, where the striking designs caught the attention of tastemakers like Sister Parish. The quilts went on to sell at Bloomingdale’s and Saks Fifth Avenue.

“The Quilts of Gee's Bend” exhibit at the Corcoran Gallery of Art in Washington, DC, in 2004

The art world caught up decades later, when a landmark exhibition, “The Quilts of Gee’s Bend,” opened at the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, in 2002, introducing the quilters to audiences far beyond Alabama. Today, their work is celebrated for its bold colors, inventive patterns, and astonishing craftsmanship. In 2006, 10 of the quilts appeared on US postage stamps. And this summer, Ralph Lauren launched a limited-edition collection of apparel, quilts, and home goods featuring designs by quilters Claudia Pettway Charley and Loretta Pettway Bennett.

But for design lovers, the festival offers something no museum can: the chance to see the quilts in the place they were made, and to meet the individual women who made them. They’re still sewn by hand, too. “[An authentic] Gee’s Bend quilt is not quilted by a sewing machine,” Mary Margaret says. “And it’s important to understand that every quilt is not alike. Everyone who quilts is not alike.”

Our quilting class ends the way it began, with plenty of laughter as we tie off our last stitches. Everyone wants a photo with Doris and Mary Margaret, and a few students have even brought books featuring the quilters’ work to be signed.

Outside, the festival is in full swing, with more than 40 booths devoted to quilters selling their quilts and wall hangings, along with puzzles and notebooks printed with Gee’s Bend patterns, doormats, quilted totes, and pot holders.

Last year’s festival drew more than 2,500 people and over $870,000 in visitor spending for the state, and Mary Margaret says guests come from as far as France and England. “They want to immerse themselves in Gee’s Bend,” she says. Doris looks forward to it all year. “I get to meet a lot of people I’ve never seen before,” she says. This year, she was especially excited to meet a 97-year-old quilter from Marion, Alabama, whose work she admires.

I’ve visited plenty of places where Black history is told in the past tense, on plaques and behind glass. Gee’s Bend feels different. Here, the history is alive, and the people who inherited it are setting the terms. That hasn’t always been easy. Over the years, says Mary Margaret, quilters have seen their work copied and sold without receiving compensation. The festival allows the public to buy directly from the quilters, at their booths or even from their porches, and know that the money is going straight to the artists.

Mostly, my day with the women of Gee’s Bend feels like a family reunion. The experience takes me straight back to childhood afternoons with my grandmother, who taught me to mend holes in pockets, sew patches onto my jeans jacket, and replace a button before anyone noticed it was missing.

Mary Margaret started even younger than I did, and now her own son and daughter are quilters themselves, working with patterns passed down through generations of the family. “To me a quilt says home,” says Mary Margaret. “It says warmth. It says care. It says time.”

#4844. 3 Training Tips That Can Help You Build Max Muscle at (and Over) 50

You can still make big gains. Here's how.

THERE ARE THINGS in your life that will change as you age. That's especially the case once you pass the half-century mark. After all the accumulated mileage of your 20s, 30s, and 40s, with the small nicks and scrapes that pile up over the years, those changes might be that you move a bit slower, or you don't bounce back as quickly. This is totally normal. You might need to ease up on some aspects of your fitness practice—but you shouldn't be discouraged. You don't have to give up on your goals. You just need to reframe your approach, since you can still make gains after 50.

The key is to be smart—and smart training follows a plan for longevity. You'll have just that with the super-popular MH MVP Premium Max Muscle at 50 program. Series creator Bryan Krahn, C.S.C.S. is a veteran trainer who knows what it takes to keep guys moving and healthy as they get older. He's his own proof of concept. He's in his 50s himself, and uses the same principles behind the program in his own workouts.

Follow the tips from Krahn below to continue building muscle and strength into your sixth decade on Earth and be sure to check out his entire Max Muscle at 50 workout program here.

Lifting heavy can be a young man's game. Krahn isn't saying that you should never pick up a big weight again—only that you can safeguard your joints by going lighter. You can still make gains this way, too. Krahn notes that studies suggest that you can still build muscle with higher rep rangers, up to 30 per set.

"Lighter weights will pack on size, as long as they make you work," he says. "So aim to use a weight that will push you when you're hitting 15 to 20 rep sets."

Krahn wants you to know that the myth of the fragile over-50 guy is a load of bunk. He says you should be doing more, if anything, not less. The key is that you shouldn't be crushing yourself with every workout.

His advice: Hit two or three hard training days per week. For the remainder of the time, stay active. Go on a run or walk, take a yoga class, or opt for your other favorite method of moving.

You can still train hard and make gains, yes—but you need to remember that your body has accrued significant mileage, so there's bound to be some wear and tear. You'll have to make more adjustments in your routine than you did when you were younger to stay in the game, so don't be afraid to shift your schedule as needed.

Be smart and listen to your body. Take days off when you need them, and don't be afraid to swap out exercises when you're not feeling 100 percent with a particular movement.

#4842. Tesla Cybercab has crashed 8 times, and the data shows a speed problem

Tesla’s Cybercab now has 8 crashes on file with NHTSA, barely two months after the purpose-built robotaxi started giving public rides in Austin.

Four happened in driverless “Robotaxi” service, and none topped 5 mph. The other four happened with a test driver on board and Tesla’s driver-assist engaged, including one where a Cybercab hit a car at 53 mph on a highway in Philadelphia.

The data points at what we think is the biggest limitation of Tesla’s self-driving program right now: speed.

Tesla files Cybercab crashes under NHTSA’s Standing General Order in two separate datasets.

The first is the ADS (Automated Driving System) file, which covers Level 4 driverless operation. That’s the Robotaxi service, where nobody is in the driver’s seat. NHTSA’s latest ADS release, published this month, contains 43 unique Tesla reports, up from 22 in July. Four are Cybercabs:

Those are minor. Two weren’t Tesla’s fault at all, and none involved an injury.

The second bucket is the Level 2 ADAS file, which covers driver-assist systems like Autopilot and “Full Self-Driving” (Supervised). Tesla has been testing Cybercabs fitted with steering wheels and a human behind them, often in places where it has no Robotaxi permit. Those crashes land in the ADAS file, with the driver type coded “In-Vehicle (Commercial / Test)” and the system “Verified Engaged.”

There are four of them, all in September 2026:

Tesla redacted the narrative of all four as confidential business information, so there’s no way to tell from the public data who was at fault or what the system was doing. Pennsylvania State Police, Austin Police, Lehi Police, and Florida Highway Patrol are listed as the investigating agencies.

The Philadelphia crash is not the Broad Street crash where a Cybercab lost its door panel that we reported in October. That one happened on a city street in October. This one happened on a highway in September, at around 10 p.m. local time.

Tesla has no permit to run automated vehicles in Pennsylvania, and it doesn’t run Robotaxi in Utah either. In Utah, a Cybercab was photographed in Park City in September with a driver visible behind the wheel.

Two of the eight Cybercab crashes involved injuries. Both are in the Level 2 file.

Across all 43 Tesla Robotaxi reports in the ADS file, the highest pre-crash speed is 29 mph. That was a driverless Model Y with two riders hitting a pothole in Dallas in September, after which one rider said they sought medical care. The median speed across all 43 reports is 1 mph.

Not one of those 43 crashes happened on a highway. Tesla coded 21 on streets, 15 in parking lots, and 7 at intersections.

Those numbers say more about where Tesla lets the system drive than about the software itself. As we reported last month, Robotaxi sticks to low-speed routes inside small geofenced zones and largely stays off highways.

The Robotaxi Safety Report Tesla published on October 21 claims zero people injured by Robotaxi over 3,112,541 driverless miles between January 22 and October 18. It doesn’t mention the Cybercab’s test fleet, and it excludes every mile driven with a safety monitor on board.

Take the speed cap off and the picture changes.

In the Level 2 data, Teslas with Autopilot or FSD engaged regularly crash at highway speeds. Our master dataset of Tesla’s ADAS reports holds 69 fatal crashes. Among the 52 where Tesla recorded a speed, the median was 53 mph, the same speed the Cybercab was going in Philadelphia, and 29 happened at 50 mph or more.

Today alone, we matched three fatal crashes to Tesla’s latest filings:

Engagement within 30 seconds of a crash, which is what triggers these reports, doesn’t prove the system caused it. But the pattern is consistent. At low speeds in a tight geofence, Tesla’s crashes are scrapes with chains, curbs, and potholes. At highway speeds, they can kill.

The Cybercab test fleet is where those two worlds overlap. It’s the same vehicle Tesla runs driverless in Austin, and the one Cybercab crash on record at real speed happened at 53 mph on a Philadelphia highway.

The Cybercab’s four driverless crashes are minor, and some weren’t Tesla’s fault. No one is denying that. But minor crashes still count, and so do the four Level 2 crashes that Tesla’s “zero injuries” framing leaves out. Both datasets describe the same vehicle running Tesla’s self-driving software.

It's looked to me for a while now that many of the improvements that people feel when they use FSD is not just the system getting better, but Elon pulling off the guardrails so the system attempts to do more stuff.

What the data shows is that Tesla has a speed problem. Its Robotaxi service looks clean largely because Tesla keeps it slow, off highways, and inside small zones. That’s also what makes it far less useful than a real ride-hailing service. You can’t take a Cybercab to the airport if the airport is on the other side of a freeway.

To be clear, we think Tesla is right to do it this way. Given what the Level 2 data shows at 50+ mph, letting driverless Cybercabs onto highways today would be reckless.

But it means the hard part is still ahead. Highways, larger geofences, and higher speeds are where crashes become fatal, and that’s where Tesla needs its system to be nearly perfect before it can scale. The Cybercab’s test crashes suggest it isn’t there yet. The question is how long Tesla can keep growing a robotaxi network that can’t go fast.

#4840. Inside Sam Bankman-Fried’s $35 Million Bahamas Crypto HQ

Four years after the fall of cryptocurrency partners-in-crime Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison, their Icarian story is coming to the small screen twice over. A docuseries about the scandal, The Boy Who Stole Millions?, debuts on Prime Video November 30, and Netflix’s drama series The Altruists premiered November 19.

No matter which retelling you tune into, much of the action is sure to take place at Bankman-Fried’s $35 million “crypto frat house” (as CNBC once called it) in The Bahamas, which served as the headquarters of his cryptocurrency exchange FTX at the time of his and Ellison’s arrests for wire fraud and several conspiracy charges in 2022.

The Orchid building at Albany, The Bahamas

Bankman-Fried and Ellison met while working at trading firm Jane Street in Manhattan in 2016, and began an on-again, off-again romantic relationship. Bankman-Fried’s first crypto business was the quantitative trading firm he cofounded in 2017, Alameda Research. He went on to found crypto exchange FTX. Ellison, who first began working at Alameda in 2018, became its co-CEO and ran the firm as FTX’s hedge fund.

Bankman-Fried and Ellison moved to The Bahamas in 2021, reportedly motivated by looser COVID-19 pandemic protocols, and “a proactive stance taken by The Bahamas and its regulatory bodies on cryptocurrencies,” Bankman-Fried told Blockworks.

Bankman-Fried shared his 11,500-square-foot unit with Ellison and eight other FTX and Alameda employees. The apartment has a circular living room, a light-up bar, Italian marble floors, cove lighting, and custom closets. Per a real estate listing obtained by Semafor, Bankman-Fried’s unit had German-engineered windows and doors. Outdoor amenities included a firepit, spa, grill and cooking area, and pool.

The couple attempted to evade culpability for misappropriating $8 billion of FTX customer money, a crime uncovered after Bankman-Fried bought his Bahamas property. Both were convicted of wire fraud and several conspiracy charges. Ellison served 14 months of a 24-month sentence. Bankman-Fried is currently serving a 25-year prison sentence and maintains that he is innocent.

To bring this story to life for The Altruists, production designer Todd Fjelsted re-created the infamous penthouse. Several interiors were shot in Vancouver, but scenes requiring a beach or docks were shot in the Dominican Republic.

Julia Garner as Caroline Ellison in a scene from The Altruists filmed in the Orchid set

Fjelsted and his crew also built miniature replicas of real Albany buildings and a marina complete with a 10-foot remote-control yacht, using forced perspective to shoot them as backdrops. He calls this “the anti-AI set.”

In the dramatization, coworkers trade crypto in a communal office and party on a balcony overlooking the water. An employee in a hot tub bangs a gong for rounds of speed chess played on fancy sets. Inside, gaming is a major pastime, and there’s a baby grand piano on hand, though no one plays it. In real life, it was reported that Bankman-Fried kept a bean bag under the piano for napping.

Alex Lawther as Sam Trabucco and Anthony Boyle as Sam Bankman-Fried in The Altruists

Looking to humanize the leads, Fjelsted observed how “insecurities [and] their feelings of a little bit of an imposter syndrome” informed Sam and Caroline’s design choices or lack thereof. Neutrals, sea colors, and palm tree prints made for a better on-camera look, but in real FBI interior photos, Fjelsted saw bedroom walls with powder blue sponge-painted over navy.

Garner and Boyle as Ellison and Bankman-Fried in The Altruists

Throughout the show’s eight episodes, the penthouse goes from bustling with the excitement of trading to vibrating with panic as the scandal comes crashing down. Eventually, the space is left nearly empty, with just Bankman-Fried and his parents remaining. In 2024, it was reported that Bankman-Fried’s real estate holdings would be sold off in order to pay back his debts, and today, the unit is indeed up for sale.

#4839. The '20-5-3' Rule Prescribes How Much Time to Spend Outside

Americans today spend 92 percent of their time indoors, and their physical and mental health are suffering. Use this three-number formula to make yourself stronger and happier.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

THE HERD OF 400-pound caribou was running 50 miles an hour and directly at me. The 30 animals had been eating lichen in the Arctic tundra in Alaska when something spooked them. I was sitting in their escape route. The ground began to vibrate once they cracked 100 yards. At 50 yards, I could see their hooves smashing the ground and kicking up moss and moisture. Then they were at 40 yards, then 35.

I could hear their breathing, smell their coats, and see all the details of their ornate antlers. Just as I was wondering if the rescue plane would be able to spot my hoof-pocked corpse, one of the caribou noticed me and swerved. The herd followed, shaking the earth as they swept left and summited a hillcrest, their antlers black against a gold sky.

That moment when those caribou shook the earth also shook my soul. It was transcendent, wild as a religious experience. And it’s not even the most intense thing I did in Alaska. I experienced savage weather, crossed raging rivers, and faced a half-ton grizzly. My brain was feeling less hunkered down in its typical foxhole—a state I’d compare to that of a roadrunner on meth, dementedly zooming from one thing to the next. My mind felt more like it belonged to a monk after a month at a meditation retreat. I just felt . . . better. The biologist E. O. Wilson put what I was feeling this way: “Nature holds the key to our aesthetic, intellectual, cognitive, and even spiritual satisfaction.”

When I returned from the wild, my Zen-like buzz hung around for months. To understand what was happening, I met with Rachel Hopman, Ph.D., a neuroscientist at Northeastern University. She told me about the nature pyramid. Think of it like the food pyramid, except that instead of recommending you eat this many servings of vegetables and this many of meat, it recommends the amount of time you should spend in nature to reduce stress and be healthier. Learn and live by the 20-5-3 rule.

THAT’S THE AMOUNT of time you should spend outside in nature, like a neighborhood park, three times a week. Hopman led a new study that concluded that something as painless as a 20-minute stroll through a city botanical garden can boost cognition and memory as well as improve feelings of well-being. “But,” she said, “we found that people who used their cell phone on the walk saw none of those benefits.”

Other research discovered that 20 minutes outside three times a week is the dose of nature that had the greatest effect on reducing an urban dweller’s levels of the stress hormone cortisol.

In nature, our brains enter a mode called “soft fascination.” Hopman described it as a mindfulness-like state that restores and builds the resources you need to think, create, process information, and execute tasks. It’s mindfulness without the meditation. A short daily nature walk—or even a walk down a tree-lined street—is a great option for people who aren’t keen on sitting and focusing on their breath. But turn off your phone—alerts from it can kick you out of soft-fascination mode.

THE MINIMUM LENGTH of time each month you should spend in semi-wild nature, like a forested state park. “Spending more time in wilder spaces does seem to give you more benefits,” said Hopman.

A 2005 survey conducted in Finland found that city dwellers felt better with at least five hours of nature a month, with benefits increasing at higher exposures. They were also more likely to be happier and less stressed in their everyday lives.

The Finnish government then funded another study in 2014 in which the scientists dumped people in a city center, a city park, and a forested state park. The two parks felt more Zen than the city center. No shocker. Except that those walking in a state park had an edge over the city-park people. They felt even more relaxed and restored. The takeaway: The wilder the nature, the better.

Nature has these effects on the mind and body because it stimulates and soothes us in unusual and unique ways. For instance, in nature you are engulfed in fractals, suggested Hopman. Fractals are complex patterns that repeat over and over in different sizes and scales and make up the design of the universe. Think: trees (big branch to smaller branch to smaller branch and so on), river systems (big river to smaller river to stream and so on), mountain ranges, clouds, seashells. “Cities don’t have fractals,” said Hopman. “Imagine a typical building. It’s usually flat, with right angles. It’s painted some dull color.” Fractals are organized chaos, which our brains apparently dig. In fact, scientists at the University of Oregon discovered that Jackson Pollock’s booze-and-jazz-fueled paintings are made up of fractals. This may explain why they speak to humans at such a core level.

Nature lifts us in other ways, too: Think smells and sounds. The feeling of the sun’s warm rays. Or just the fact that you’re getting out of the stress of your home or office. “It’s probably a mix of a lot of things,” said Hopman. Environments like cities, with their frenetic pace, right angles, loud noises, rotten smells, pinging phones, and to-do lists, don’t offer this.

THIS IS THE TOP OF THE PYRAMID. Three is the number of days you should spend each year off the grid in nature, camping or renting a cabin (with friends or solo). Think: places characterized by spotty cell reception and wild animals, away from the hustle and bustle.

This dose of the wildest nature is sort of like an extended meditation retreat. Except talking is allowed and there are no gurus. It causes your brain to ride alpha waves, the same waves that increase during meditation or when you lapse into a flow state. They can reset your thinking, boost creativity, tame burnout, and just make you feel better.

This is likely why one study found that three days in the wild boosts creativity and problem-solving abilities and another found that U. S. military vets who spent four days white-water rafting were still buzzing off the wild a week later. Their PTSD symptoms and stress levels were down 29 and 21 percent, respectively. Their relationships, happiness, and general satisfaction with their lives all improved as well.

When I returned from Alaska, my wife and I moved to the edge of the desert in Las Vegas. She wanted a shorter commute, and I wanted more access to nature. I now walk my dogs through red-rock trails for at least 20 minutes daily and on Sunday do a long trail run deep into the canyons to rack up my five-hour quota for the month. This summer, I’m planning a weeklong backcountry fly-fishing trip in Idaho’s Frank Church–River of No Return Wilderness Area. Hoping I’ll return less frazzled, fitter, and feeling more alive.

Adapted from the book The Comfort Crisis: Embrace Discomfort to Reclaim Your Wild, Happy, Healthy Self, by Michael Easter, out now from Rodale Books. Copyright © 2021 by Michael Easter.This story appeared in the June 2021 issue of Men's Health with the title The 20-5-3 Nature Cure.

#4838. Adding wind cuts solar + battery storage power costs nearly 20%

Solar and battery storage can do a lot of the heavy lifting in a renewable electricity system. Add wind, and supplying reliable power gets nearly 20% cheaper, according to new analysis from energy think tank Ember.

Wind fills gaps when solar output drops, so the system needs fewer batteries to keep electricity flowing.

Ember’s analysis, produced with the Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC), found that adding wind to solar and battery storage cuts the median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour.

The median cost of solar and wind power covering all demand is $89/MWh, with batteries and a little backup.

Solar and wind don’t follow the same schedule. Their output varies by time of day and across seasons, allowing one to offset the other’s shortfalls.

That matters because storing enough electricity to get through a long stretch of weak solar output gets expensive. Wind reduces the amount of energy the batteries need to store in the first place.

In the US, adding wind reduces the modeled battery requirement to meet 90% of demand from 20 hours of electricity use to 12 hours. Europe sees the same reduction, while China’s requirement falls from 18 hours to 12.

The savings also put cheaper renewable power within reach of more regions. With wind included, regions that account for 75% of global electricity demand can meet 90% of their electricity demand at less than $100/MWh. With solar and batteries alone, that share is only 50%.

“We already know that solar and wind are cheap,” said Daan Walter, principal at Ember.

By combining solar, wind, and batteries, we can deliver reliable power at remarkably low costs almost everywhere in the world. That’s a pretty fundamental shift in the economics of energy.

The researchers also looked at prolonged periods of low output. Globally, weighted by electricity demand, a week of low solar output occurs roughly four times a year. A week in which both solar and wind output are low occurs only about once every four years.

That’s a global average, so individual locations will have different experiences. Ember defines a lull as seven consecutive days of output below half the source’s average.

Combining wind and solar reduces the gaps in low output.

The findings also raise questions for developers planning new fossil fuel plants.

Ember identifies 845 GW of coal and gas capacity in planning worldwide. Adding wind raises the share located in regions where solar, wind, and battery storage can meet 90% of demand for under $100/MWh from 71% to 90%.

In China alone, wind brings another 91 GW of planned coal and gas capacity into the range where renewables are cheaper.

Include backup to cover all demand, and 706 GW of the planned fossil fuel capacity sits in regions where the renewable-based alternative costs less than $100/MWh. Without wind, that figure falls to 520 GW.

For investors financing fossil fuel plants in the pipeline that are expected to run for decades, there is likely already a cheaper renewable alternative available to meet the same electricity demand, so it’s worth scrutinizing the project’s economics.

This works even better with greater efficiency on the consumption side of the equation.

#4834. Netflix’s The Altruists Tells a Compelling Story of Love, Money, and Fraud. Here’s What Really Happened.

The true story behind Sam Bankman-Fried, Caroline Ellison, and the $8 billion crypto collapse is even messier than the show lets on.

NETFLIX’S LATEST HEADLINE-MAKING limited series The Altruists has a lot of big names attached to it. There are Irish and American actors Anthony Boyle and Julia Garner, respectively, playing up their dorkiest selves to portray Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison. (Ostensibly while Garner desperately awaits casting in a possible Madonna biopic that has been in development hell for what feels like forever.)

Who, you ask? Well, if you’ve avoided the cryptocurrency market and carbon-positive NFT gorillas in the past several years, we can’t really blame you. But what you need to know is that Bankman-Fried and Ellison were the heads of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX as well as lovers. FTX, and the love between them, notoriously collapsed when Bankman-Fried was arrested and accused of stealing over $8 billion in customer funds.

Why is this story about fraud (of which Bankman-Fried was eventually convicted) called The Altruists? Ironically, FTX was purportedly created as a company that gave away as much as it earned, based on the principle of effective altruism—words that got everyone in the finance world hot and heavy with excitement. Until news came out that Bankman-Fried and other FTX executives had spent billion-dollar-sized wads of cash “on luxury hotel stays, private planes, DoorDash orders, trips to Jimmy Buffett's Margaritaville, and, in the case of one top executive, a $2.5 million yacht,” Business Insider reports. FTX was also known for hosting an ultra-luxe conference in the Bahamas that featured famous folks including Bill Clinton, Tom Brady, and the musicians Steve Aoki and the late Liam Payne of One Direction, who in 2024 fell to his death from a hotel balcony in Argentina at the age of 31.

So, yeah, we’re dealing with a twisted and extremely millennial story full of curveballs and screwballs. But whether you’re watching The Altruists or simply hearing about it, what do you need to know about the true FTX story at the heart of it? We’ve got you covered below.

The Altruists is as much a love story as it is a story of financial doom: The two were intertwined with Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison, who met at an investment firm and fell in love. Bankman-Fried would found FTX as well as its sister cryptocurrency trading firm Alameda Research, while Ellison was CEO of Alameda Research, which funneled money from FTX.

FTX was on an upward trajectory in the early 2020s, garnering Bankman-Fried the nickname of “Crypto King.” The company, once worth $32 billion, nosedived into bankruptcy in 2022 while also being investigated by the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Justice Department. Bankman-Fried “sounded surprisingly calm” in an interview with The New York Times amid FTX’s freefall. “You would’ve thought that I’d be getting no sleep right now, and instead I’m getting some,” he told the publication. “It could be worse.”

Yes. In fact, things could and did get a lot worse for this once seemingly altruistic finance dude. He and Ellison broke off their romantic relationship amid FTX’s collapse in 2022. (“She wanted more from it than I was able to give,” Bankman-Fried testified, according to the Wall Street Journal. To which one can only wonder: More than $8 billion?)

On March 28, 2024, Bankman-Fried was sentenced to 25 years in prison, three years of supervised release, and was additionally ordered to “pay $11 billion in forfeiture for his orchestration of multiple fraudulent schemes,” the Justice Department announced.

In total, he was convicted of two counts of wire fraud, two counts of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, one count of conspiracy to commit securities fraud, and one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering.

What’s curious is that his right-hand woman, Ellison, only got less than two years in prison for her part in the cryptocurrency fraud, though she did plead guilty to two counts of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, two counts of wire fraud, one count of conspiracy to commit commodities fraud, one count of conspiracy to commit securities fraud, and one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering. She was also ordered to forfeit $11 billion.

Her relatively light sentence can be explained by the fact that, though the “very math-y” Stanford graduate helped orchestrate the multibillion-dollar scheme alongside Bankman-Fried, she became a star witness for the prosecution against her former boyfriend. The prosecutors offered her a sweetened deal to shorten her prison time in exchange for cooperation, information, and testimony.

She testified, NPR reports, that as Alameda found itself in a financial hole, Bankman-Fried directed her to take more money from FTX customers to bail the company out. “We were in a bad situation,” she said.

U.S. Attorney Damian Williams said of Bankman-Fried’s scheme that it was “one of the largest financial frauds in history, stealing over $8 billion of his customers’ money.”

Their love may be over, and they are both convicted felons, all of which gets packed into the final episode of the eight-part The Altruists. But at least Ellison is moving on. Sort of. After being imprisoned for less than two years, she is now a free woman.

In September, Ellison formally joined Manifund “to develop our funding platform and research how to effectively direct philanthropic dollars,” the company’s CEO Austin Chen announced, per Oxygen. She had reportedly joined the nonprofit funding platform and philanthropic organization on a trial basis at first and went by the innocent-sounding pseudonym “Carol.” This work is in line with her stated belief in effective altruism, which in turn became a multibillion-dollar con, which doesn’t sound all that altruistic or effective.

“On FTX itself, I remain conflicted. It was their money and spirit that enabled the Future Fund, and I still admire many aspects of FTX and the individuals who worked there,” Chen wrote. “But also: FTX did wrong. Its collapse harmed users (myself included), and damaged the movement which I deeply care about.”

Chen is a big believer in redemption. “I’d like to give her the opportunity to contribute back to the world,” he wrote. “I hope that the world will concur.” Which is very generous of him. Maybe she’ll even get a Nathan Fielder-hosted documentary one day.

Bankman-Fried, meanwhile? He’s still behind bars on that 25-year sentence. Thankfully for him, however, he is incarcerated at the low-security California federal prison Federal Correctional Institution Lompoc, which is known for its open dormitory and room-type housing.

Maybe he will find a new way to be altruistic. Or, at least, stop committing federal crimes.

#4833. Your First Look at 7th Avenue's First NYC Showroom

You don't need much of an imagination to picture yourself curled up on one of 7th Avenue's sectionals. One look at the extra deep seats and plush cushions is enough to have you planning your movie marathon—pass the popcorn, please. But even so, a couch is the sort of thing you want to try before you buy. With the opening of a new flagship showroom in New York City's SoHo neighborhood, the brand is hoping you'll make a day of it; get comfortable, stay a while.

This month, 7th Avenue cut the ribbon on a 3,240-square-foot storefront in a historic cast-iron building at 476 Broome Street. It's the 30th brick-and-mortar space in the US and first permanent location in NYC to open since the brand's founding as a direct-to-consumer business in 2022. Co-founder and CEO Billy Shaw says that he and co-founder Josh Stinson decided to put down roots in the Big Apple after seeing the way New Yorkers took to their hero product—the "World's Greatest Modular Sofa," they call it—during the years they operated a pop-up shop in the city.

“The main showroom celebrates volume and openness, with soaring ceilings, dramatic columns, and refined architectural detailing,” says Stinson.

Co-founders Stinson and Shaw sourced design details for the showroom from around the world. “[These items] have an Old-World patina that balances the modern, contemporary aesthetics of our sofas,” says Shaw.

"We were inspired to create 7th Avenue to solve for a frustration we kept hearing from customers: Finding a sofa that was both beautifully designed and genuinely practical for everyday living was surprisingly difficult," Shaw says. (The brand famously uses water-repellent and stain-resistant performance fabrics, and all sofa covers can be removed and thrown in the washing machine for cleaning.) New Yorkers appreciated the modular designs, which can fit into petite elevators and through the narrow doors and hallways ubiquitous in city homes (gotta love a pre-war building!). “Our sofas arrive in individual boxes, making those tight spaces easier to navigate,” he adds.

A store in New York was a no-brainer, but that doesn't mean finding a location was easy. Shaw and Stinson, who is COO, considered addresses in the Flatiron District, where shoppers can bop in and out of home retailers—like Herman Miller, Design Within Reach, ABC Carpet & Home, Crate & Barrel, the list goes on—without leaving a three-block radius. But ultimately they couldn't let go of SoHo's "unmatched" energy. "We wanted to find a place that is grand and historic, paying homage to NYC’s architectural heritage," says Stinson. With 14-foot ceilings and a skylight, "the space on Broome Street creates a sense of openness and grandeur from the moment customers walk through the door."

Just how durable are 7th Avenue's furniture pieces? During the SoHo store's opening party, guests were encouraged to drop their drinks on the sofas in a “spill lab.”

Shaw and Stinson, who designed the space themselves, say they used the building's architecture to create different vignettes and experiences for guests. The main showroom, for instance, with its dramatic columns and open space, is perfect for showing off 7th Avenue's larger sectionals. Elsewhere, a daybed is nestled into an alcove for a more intimate scene. "We wanted to demonstrate that great furniture design isn't simply about size," says Stinson. "It's about proportion and the relationship between a piece and the space surrounding it."

The two also wanted to show that "beautiful design should work for real life." "That meant balancing the stateliness of the cast-iron architecture and high ceilings with warm materials, organic textures, and comfortable places to sit," says Shaw.

A light and bright backdrop of European oak and Turkish travertine is dotted with treasures gathered from around the world: coral stone coffee tables quarried from volcanic islands in Indonesia, century-old olive oil jars from Turkey and Morocco, sculptural plants like a Hawaiian dragon tree. "A Queensland Bottle Tree Bonsai, native to Australia and sourced from Los Angeles plant specialists The Plant Daddies, was shaped over two years to achieve its distinctive curved form," says Stinson. These details, Shaw adds, have "an Old-World patina that balances the modern, contemporary aesthetics of our sofas."

Guests readily settled into 7th Avenue's plush sofas at the flagship's opening party.

"We want customers to feel comfortable settling into this beautiful sofa, yet imagining it in their own home and being used in their day-to-day lives," says Stinson. At the opening party, props scattered about the furniture brought this idea to life.

For all the finery, 476 Broome Street feels more like someone's home than an art gallery—and that's very on purpose. "We want customers to feel comfortable settling into this beautiful sofa, yet imagining it in their own home and being used in their day-to-day lives," says Stinson. The co-founders want visitors to interact with the furniture. Indeed, a cheeky neon sign that reads "Come Spill on Me" hangs over an emerald velvet couch; at the store's opening party, red wine was passed with nonchalance and guests were invited to plop onto a double-wide sofa and pose for photos with an artful disarray of newspapers, a pizza box, and an overturned gag martini glass—no need to take their shoes off.

According to Shaw and Stinson, great design should accommodate the realities of modern life, messy things like kids, pets, and parties. "Our clients appreciate beautiful, thoughtfully designed spaces, but they also want to live in them without hesitation," says Shaw. "Ultimately, we feel that luxury should be lived in, not simply admired."

#4831. Tesla needs wireless charging fast, or its $30,000 Cybercab can’t charge at home

Tesla is now taking orders for the $29,990 Cybercab, with the first deliveries expected in Austin next month. But there’s a problem buyers should know about: they won’t be able to charge it at home.

The Cybercab has no onboard charger, so it only takes DC fast charging. And the wireless home charging pad Tesla has been teasing since 2023 still isn’t something you can buy.

When Tesla unveiled the Cybercab in 2024, Elon Musk said it wouldn’t even have a plug. “It just goes over the inductive charger and charges,” he said on stage.

That plan didn’t survive production, or at least the current version in production. Cybercabs have a NACS charge port behind a panel in the rear bumper, and Tesla has been plugging Cybercabs into regular Superchargers in Austin since they joined the fleet.

The bigger issue is what sits behind that port. Tesla confirmed to attendees at Tesla’s Austin launch event in September that Cybercab has no onboard charger, the box that turns the AC power coming out of your wall into DC power the battery can store.

No onboard charger means no Wall Connector. No Mobile Connector on a 120V outlet, and no Level 2 station at the mall either. If it isn’t a DC fast charger, the Cybercab can’t use it.

For a robotaxi, deleting the onboard charger makes sense. It’s one less part to buy, cool, and carry around, and a fleet car spends its downtime at a depot, not in someone’s garage. Those little things help make the car more economical and efficient.

But Tesla is now selling the Cybercab to individuals.

As we reported last week, Tesla’s Cybercab autonomy agreement requires a $299 monthly subscription for the car to move at all. The same document puts charging squarely on the buyer: “You are responsible for registration, insurance, parking, charging, general cleaning and all other costs.”

It also tells owners to “keep the vehicle charged and connected so over-the-air updates can install.” Connected to what, it doesn’t say.

The Cybercab Order Agreement limits the car to NACS DC fast charging, Superchargers included. It also says only the registered owner can use the Cybercab, and only while physically present in it for the entire trip.

The subscription agreement carves out one exception: when service is due, the Cybercab “will travel autonomously, unoccupied to a Tesla service center.” Nothing similar exists for charging.

So you can’t send your Cybercab to a Supercharger at 2 a.m. while you sleep, which is the one thing a self-driving car should be great at. You’d have to ride along, sit in a two-seater at a Supercharger while it charges, and ride back home.

The obvious answer is the wireless home charger Tesla keeps promising.

Tesla first showed what looked like a wireless home charging station during its Investor Day in March 2023. Later that year, chief designer Franz von Holzhausen confirmed the project on Jay Leno’s Garage, saying owners would “just drive over the pad in your garage” to start charging.

Tesla then filed patents for the charging pad and, after the Cybercab unveiling, released a video of it charging the robotaxi at 25 kW, claiming efficiency “well above 90%.” In February, the FCC granted Tesla a waiver to use ultra-wideband radios to guide the Cybercab onto the pad.

And that’s where it stops. Tesla has never sold the pad, never priced it, and never given it a launch date. It even gave up on wireless charging for the Cybertruck last year, even though the truck shipped with the connectors for it.

With deliveries estimated for December, Tesla has about six weeks to launch a home pad if it wants the first owners to charge in their own garage.

Tesla’s own plans for Cybercab charging revolve around fleet depots. In Austin, it filed plans for a hub on St. Elmo Road with 48 V4 Supercharger stalls in a first phase and cabinets to support 80 wireless chargers in a second.

Tesla could, in theory, let private owners use it. But with the owner-presence rule, that means riding to a depot across town and waiting there. That’s a Supercharger visit with extra steps.

The other route is a home DC charger, and those exist. We covered Sigenergy’s 25 kW bidirectional DC charging module last year, which bypasses a car’s onboard charger the same way a Supercharger does. Lunar Energy also announced a 25 kW home DC charger this year, but it’s not expected until mid-2027.

Neither is a plug-and-play answer. Sigenergy’s module is built to sit inside its SigenStor home battery system, which isn’t cheap, and Tesla would have to support third-party DC charging on a car it controls this tightly. Tesla could also build its own small DC wall unit. It hasn’t announced one, but CEO Elon Musk talked about integrating one into the Powerwall for years.

This is what happens when you take a vehicle designed for a fleet and sell it to consumers to hit a deadline. And let’s be honest, charging is probably not even in the top 5 of problems with selling the Cybercab to personal owners in its current state.

Musk promised a Cybercab would be sold to a customer for under $30,000 before 2027. Technically, he’s going to make it. But on the Q3 earnings call, he also said “the vast majority” of Cybercabs will stay Tesla-owned and run as transport-as-a-service. The car was clearly engineered around that, and deleting the onboard charger is the best example.

That saved Tesla money on every unit. The cost now lands on the few people buying one.

I don't see any evidence that the production Cybercab has the onboard hardware to use such a pad. Besides the wireless receiver coil it would need some kind of charging hardware to convert the pulsed wireless charging into DC to charge the battery.

If you live in Austin next to a Supercharger, you’ll manage. But think about what Tesla is actually selling here: a self-driving car that can’t drive itself to charge, can’t charge in your garage, and needs you sitting in it at a Supercharger. That’s worse than owning a Model 3 with a Wall Connector, and it costs $299 a month on top.

The fix exists in Tesla’s labs. It has the pad, the patents, and the FCC approval. It needs to ship it as a product, ideally bundled with the car, or change the contract to let the Cybercab go charge on its own.

Will the first Cybercab owners get a wireless pad in December, or will they spend their evenings at Superchargers? And if it launches, how much will it cost? The rare few home wireless chargers that have been sold to date have been quite expensive, and the value proposition of the Cybercab, which is currently basically a $300 a month lease with a $30,000 down payment, is already pretty awful.

If you’re buying an EV, how you charge it at home matters as much as the car itself, and pairing it with rooftop solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs.
